The datacom transceiver segment dwarfs everything else: LightCounting reports Ethernet transceiver sales grew 93% in 2024, ~82% in 2025, and forecasts ~65% growth in 2026, with total Ethernet transceiver + CPO/NPO sales reaching ~$26B in 2026 (from ~$16.5B in 2025). 800G+ transceiver shipments are expected to jump from ~24M units (2025) to ~63M (2026), and 1.6T chipset sales should surpass $2B in 2026 — '2026 is the year of 1.6T.' Demand currently exceeds supply by ~30%, with shortages expected to resolve by end of 2026.\n\nThe growth driver is unambiguous: AI cluster scale-out (and increasingly scale-up) bandwidth. Every GPU generation roughly doubles per-accelerator network bandwidth, and hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google) are accelerating the 400G->800G->1.6T transition. Scale-up networks (intra-rack/pod GPU-to-GPU) are emerging as an entirely new optical market — LightCounting called scale-up 'a new market for optical interconnects' in July 2025, and Broadcom's OCI MSA standard (presented at OFC 2026) targets exactly this. NVIDIA claims 3.5x network power efficiency for Quantum-X/Spectrum-X Photonics; Broadcom claims 70% power reduction for TH6-Davisson vs pluggables. However, first-gen CPO carries higher per-port cost than high-volume pluggables and sacrifices serviceability/multi-vendor sourcing, so in 2026 CPO is only ~0.5% of AI datacenter optical modules. Pluggables retain the majority of links through the decade per LightCounting, but CPO's share is projected to reach ~30% of 800G/1.6T port shipments by 2027 (some forecasts) and ~35% of AI DC optics by 2030; CPO market revenue forecasts range from $8.1B (Yole-cited, from $46M in 2024, ~137% CAGR) to $10B (LightCounting, incl. scale-up) by 2030.\n\nKey inflection points 2026-2030: (1) 2026 — 1.6T pluggable volume ramp; TSMC COUPE enters volume production; NVIDIA Quantum-X Photonics InfiniBand CPO switches ship (early 2026), Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics (409.6 Tbps) ships H2 2026; Broadcom ships third-gen Tomahawk 6-Davisson 102.4 Tbps CPO in volume. (2) 2027 — NVIDIA Rubin Ultra (late 2027) with deeper photonics integration; 1.6T reaches cost-per-bit parity with 800G. (3) 2028-2030 — large-scale CPO deployment per Yole; hyperscaler commitments for CPO-based scale-up fabrics; NVIDIA's post-Rubin 'Feynman' generation is the primary CPO focus per SemiAnalysis; optical I/O chiplets (Ayar Labs TeraPHY 8 Tbps, Lightmatter Passage L200/L200X 32/64 Tbps, Celestial/Marvell Photonic Fabric 16 Tbps chiplet) move from sampling to production; Samsung targets CPO turnkey by 2029. Non-datacom segments (telecom DWDM ~13% CAGR 2026-2031, sensing/LiDAR/biosensing, photonic computing at $2.2B in 2026 growing ~35% CAGR) are real but small relative to datacom, which was ~62% of revenue via transceivers in 2024; data center & HPC was a ~$1.3B silicon photonics segment in 2025. The critical technical bottleneck across all segments remains the laser: per Meta, ~90% of optical link failures trace to lasers and lasers consume ~60% of link power — explaining NVIDIA's laser-supplier investments and the crowded field of light-source startups (external lasers, heterogeneous InP, quantum-dot, comb lasers).",

That hyperscaler-driven MSA effectively blesses the UCIe+optics chiplet model that Ayar Labs pioneered and pressures everyone toward a multi-vendor optical-engine supply chain. Meta disclosed a 90-million-hour CPO reliability validation at OFC 2026, addressing the biggest hyperscaler objection (field reliability/serviceability).\n\nThe LPO-vs-CPO debate has resolved into a coexistence view: LPO (DSP-less linear pluggables) offers 30-50% lower power and lower cost with the pluggable serviceability model, and is penetrating 800G short-reach links now with >8M 1.6T LPO ports forecast by 2027 — but at 1.6T (>30W modules) linear-retimed optics (LRO) looks more practical, and pluggables of all types are still expected to dominate volumes through ~2027, with CPO reaching roughly 30% of 800G/1.6T port shipments in 2027 and dominating 100T+ switch generations after that. What remains unsolved: laser integration and placement (industry consensus is external laser sources — lasers plus TECs are ~70% of ELS power draw and links need ~24.5 dBm launch power to cover connector/coupling/modulator losses); serviceability (a failed optical engine can scrap a whole ASIC package — mitigations are detachable optical subassemblies like Nvidia's six 4.8 Tbps OSAs per Quantum-X switch and front-panel ELSFP lasers); thermals (photonics co-located with 1kW+ ASICs, forcing liquid cooling on all announced CPO switches); and fiber attach/packaging yield at volume, which is why TSMC's COUPE (volume production 2026) and the Amkor/ASE-class OSAT ecosystem are the real bottleneck. Samsung is roughly 3 years behind TSMC (CPO turnkey targeted 2029).\n\nWho is winning: Broadcom on shipping switch CPO today; Nvidia on captive volume (its own switches plus $4B supply-chain lock-in) and on setting the scale-up agenda via NVLink Fusion; TSMC as the near-monopoly foundry layer; Marvell bought its way into scale-up optics via Celestial AI; Ayar Labs is the best-positioned independent optical-chiplet vendor (Nvidia, AMD, Intel all invested; NVLink Fusion member); Lightmatter is the interposer-architecture outlier now testing public markets. Silicon photonics in mid-2026 is a market with one overwhelming demand engine — AI datacenter interconnect — and everything else orbiting it. Yole puts the overall market at $3.9B (2025) with silicon-photonics modules growing from $4.2B (2024) to $24.8B (2030); LightCounting shows Ethernet transceiver sales growing 93%/82%/65% in 2024/2025/2026 with demand exceeding supply by ~30%. 2026 is 'the year of 1.6T': 800G+ shipments jump from ~24M to ~63M units. Co-packaged optics has crossed from demo to deployment — Broadcom's Tomahawk 6-Davisson shipping in volume, NVIDIA's Quantum-X/Spectrum-X Photonics landing in 2026 on TSMC COUPE — but CPO is still only ~0.5% of AI DC optics today, forecast to reach ~30-35% of high-speed ports by 2027-2030 ($8-10B market). Pluggables (including LPO/LRO variants) keep the majority of volume through the decade.

The structural story for a founder is consolidation and vertical integration. Between late 2025 and mid-2026, more than $15B changed hands: Marvell bought Celestial AI ($3.25B, up to $5.5B), Credo bought DustPhotonics (~$1.3B), Molex bought Teramount ($430M, ten months after its $50M round), Ciena bought Nubis ($270M), AMD bought Enosemi, GlobalFoundries bought AMF and InfiniLink, and NVIDIA deployed ~$6.5B into Coherent, Lumentum and Corning to lock down laser supply. On the venture side, Ayar Labs ($500M Series E, $3.75B) and Lightmatter ($850M raised, S-1 at ~$12.5B) show the optical-I/O lane is both validated and effectively closed to new entrants at the chiplet level without $500M+ of capital. The flip side: acquirers demonstrably pay $270M-$3.25B for production-ready CPO-adjacent technology, and time-to-exit can be under four years (Teramount, Nubis, DustPhotonics, Enosemi). Strategic CVCs (NVIDIA, AMD, Cisco, Samsung, Applied, Koch) sit in nearly every cap table by Series A — plan for it.

Where the value pools have not yet been claimed is the unglamorous middle of the stack. Five hard bottlenecks bind the whole industry: (1) lasers — per Meta, ~90% of optical link failures trace to lasers and they consume ~60% of link power, with lasers + TECs eating ~70% of external-laser-source power; (2) packaging and fiber attach — 50-80% of total module cost, sub-micron alignment against an ~800x mode-size mismatch; (3) test and known-good-die — >100 seconds to inspect a single PIC, no unified standard, and a CPO package that aggregates 24+ optical engines where one bad engine scraps the assembly; (4) thermal tuning of microrings — a per-ring milliwatt heater tax (~0.12 nm/mW) that erodes the pJ/bit advantage of every ring-based DWDM link; and (5) yield/variability — photonics has no CMOS-grade statistical corner models. TSMC itself names wafer-level optical test, fiber array integration, and optical packaging as the CPO blockers. These are the picks-and-shovels lanes where a new company faces equipment incumbents (FormFactor, Teradyne, Aehr) on hardware but almost nobody on the software, analytics, and IP layers.

Software is the most striking vacuum. Within twelve months, essentially every independent photonic design software vendor was absorbed: Lumerical into Synopsys (via the $35B Ansys deal), RSoft and VPIphotonics into Keysight, Luceda into China's Semitronix, Quantifi into Teradyne. There is now no neutral, Western, cloud-native photonic EDA vendor — while 110+ US silicon photonics companies (59 VC-backed), foundries standing up PDKs (TSMC COUPE, GF Fotonix, Tower, UMC/imec), and hyperscaler CPO architecture teams all need modern tooling. Flexcompute's June 2026 autonomous agent-driven design loop and Axiomatic AI's $18M seed prove the 'AI-native photonic design' thesis is investable; the open-source gdsfactory ecosystem (2M+ downloads, essentially uncommercialized) is a ready-made distribution wedge. Photonic EDA is a small market today (~$0.4-1.3B) — the honest framing is that a software entrant is building either an acquisition target for Cadence/Keysight/Synopsys or the design-to-manufacturing data layer of a much larger test/yield business.

Photonic computing has resolved: photons win where they move data, not where they compute. Lightmatter — the best-funded compute startup — pivoted entirely to interconnect; Luminous died; Lightelligence's HK$80B IPO on ~100M yuan revenue is a hype signal, not a business signal. The genuinely commercial adjacent category is optical circuit switching: Google's Palomar OCS is worth >$3B internally, Microsoft deployed OCS across 12 Azure zones, a merchant market ($0.56B in 2026 → ~$2.5B by 2029-2032) is forming around Lumentum/Coherent/Polatis, and OCP just launched OCS standardization. Critically, the hardware is arriving before the software: non-Google operators lack Google's topology-engineering and scheduling stack, which is a classic control-plane opening.

Beyond datacom, the pattern among winners is 'sell performance to defense and industrial buyers now, ride the datacom-subsidized foundry cost curve down.' Anello's silicon-photonic gyro (a $20M DoD production award, oversubscribed round, designs into USVs/AUVs amid exploding GPS-jamming demand) is the most capital-efficient success in the whole space. FMCW LiDAR is real but consolidating around Aeva ($18.1M revenue, $127.6M operating loss — a warning about vertical integration). Consumer biosensing remains the graveyard (Rockley's >$500M burn), with SiPhox the modest exception and Apple the only potential volume driver. Quantum photonics (PsiQuantum $7B, Xanadu public) is credibly funded but pre-commercial until 2028+; its main near-term relevance to a startup is as a demanding customer for low-loss photonics, detectors, and packaging.

Net assessment for company formation in 2026: do not build another optical I/O chiplet, another analog optical AI accelerator, or a consumer photonic wearable — those lanes are respectively capital-closed, strategically abandoned, and repeatedly fatal. Do build where hyperscaler money is already committed but the supplier base is thin: design/test/yield software (greenfield, buildable this week), CPO link-level digital twins, OCS orchestration, merchant FMCW/PNT photonic engines for defense and industrial, laser reliability and thermals (the single biggest quantified pain point), and packaging/test picks-and-shovels. Entry pricing is observable — pre-seed ~€4.5M, seed $6-12M, Series A $20-80M — and the exit window for production-ready CPO-adjacent technology is short and well-priced. The theses below span that spectrum, from two-person software companies to a nine-figure deep-tech laser bet.

theses.name: Aperture (neutral, AI-native photonic EDA)
theses.one_liner: The independent, cloud-native, agentic design platform for photonic ICs — the 'Figma vs Adobe' play against the Synopsys/Keysight/Semitronix roll-ups, built open-core on gdsfactory.
theses.wedge: A solver-agnostic AI design copilot + verification layer for PIC designers: starts as enterprise tooling on top of open-source gdsfactory (2M+ downloads, de facto community standard, essentially uncommercialized by DoPlayDo) — curvilinear-aware DRC that kills false polygon-discretization errors, layout-vs-intent checking, and an agent that drives Tidy3D/MEEP/Lumerical against foundry PDKs (Tower PH18/OpenLight, GF Fotonix, imec, AIM) to produce verified, tapeout-ready GDS. First customers: the 59+ VC-backed US photonics startups and foundry design-enablement teams, all of whom face a documented PIC-designer specialization mismatch (EPIC data) and per-seat license pain from incumbents.
theses.why_now: In 12 months every independent Western photonic EDA vendor disappeared: Lumerical→Synopsys ($35B Ansys deal, July 2025), RSoft+VPIphotonics→Keysight (Oct 2025/June 2026), Luceda→China's Semitronix (Aug 2025). US hyperscalers, defense primes, and startups now have zero neutral modern option, and Luceda's Chinese ownership creates active export-control discomfort. Simultaneously, Flexcompute's June 2026 autonomous agent-driven design loop proved agentic PIC design works (but it's locked to their solver), and design-tool spending leads CPO hardware volume by 2-3 years — 2026-2027 is exactly when architecture teams staff up.
theses.market: Brutally honest: pure photonic EDA is only ~$0.4-1.3B today, growing 12-18% CAGR (vs $15B+ electronic EDA). Realistic SAM for a specialist tool vendor is maybe $150-300M near-term (datacom design teams ~42% of demand, quantum fastest-growing at 22% CAGR). So the standalone-SaaS outcome is capped around $30-80M ARR at plausible share — but that supports a $500M-1.5B strategic exit to Cadence (the one EDA major without an owned photonic physics engine), Keysight, or a foundry. The market gets bigger if you win the design-to-yield data layer (see risks/moat), because that attaches to the $14.4B-by-2031 packaging/test economy rather than seat licenses.
theses.competition: Synopsys OptoCompiler+Lumerical (dominant, but desktop-era, expensive, bundled to electronic platform deals); Keysight (assembling device-to-system stack via acquisition, strong at link level, weak at layout/agents); Cadence (partner or acquirer, not really a competitor in photonic physics); Flexcompute PhotonForge (the real threat — funded ~$80M, GPU-native, already agentic, but closed to its own solver and priced per-simulation); DoPlayDo/GDSFactory+ (same wedge, but unfunded and thinly commercialized — out-executable, or an acqui-hire); Photonium (YC, bulk optics not PICs, $660K ARR proves willingness to pay). Luceda is disqualified for US-sensitive customers by ownership.
theses.moat: Weak initially — honest assessment: agentic wrappers are copyable. Durable moat comes from three accretions: (1) becoming the community standard via open-core gdsfactory stewardship (distribution incumbents can't replicate without cannibalizing licenses); (2) foundry PDK QA relationships — being the qualified path for OpenLight/Tower/GF PDKs is a bilateral switching cost; (3) the real prize: measured-fab-data-calibrated compact models and variability/yield prediction (the exact thesis behind Semitronix buying Luceda) — proprietary silicon-correlation data compounds and is unbuyable by a late entrant.
theses.capital_intensity: Very low. 3-6 engineers, laptops, cloud GPU credits, and ~$50-100K/year of MPW seats (CORNERSTONE/imec ~$10-30K, AIM $35K+) to validate designs in silicon for credibility. Seed of $3-6M carries you to first enterprise contracts; Series A $20-30M funds foundry partnerships and a silicon-validation loop. No fab, no inventory.
theses.software_mvp: This week: fork gdsfactory; ship (a) a curvilinear-aware DRC checker that pre-legalizes inverse-designed geometry (productize OptiClear's published approach) and (b) an MCP-served agent that takes a natural-language spec ('CWDM4 mux, GF Fotonix, <1.5dB IL'), runs parameterized gdsfactory components through open-source MEEP/SAX simulation, iterates, and emits DRC-clean GDS with a verification report. Demo against a public PDK (SiEPIC/CORNERSTONE); post it where the 80+ funded photonics startups' designers live. Paying design-services engagements can start in month one.
risks: Small TAM ceiling: photonic EDA seats may never support a venture-scale standalone outcome — this is plausibly a $300M-1B exit, not an IPO; investors must underwrite accordingly
Flexcompute gets there first with $80M and a head start on agentic design; Cadence could also partner with them instead of you
Foundries (TSMC especially) keep leading-edge PDKs closed — you may be locked out of the COUPE ecosystem where the biggest customers design
Open-core is hard: gdsfactory community goodwill can be squandered, and DoPlayDo already occupies the commercial position nominally
Incumbents bundle photonics into electronic platform deals at effectively zero marginal price, suppressing your pricing

theses.name: Interferon (CPO digital twin + test/yield data layer)
theses.one_liner: Cloud software that predicts, tests, and certifies co-packaged optics — link-level E-O-E digital twins for CPO architects plus known-good-optical-engine analytics for the test floor.
theses.wedge: Two-sided entry, one data model. Side A: a statistically-aware (Monte Carlo corner) link simulator spanning SerDes→optical engine→fiber plant→receiver with BER/power/thermal prediction, sold via API to CPO system architecture teams at switch/XPU vendors and hyperscalers. Side B: test-content and analytics software sitting on top of the probe hardware incumbents (Teradyne/ficonTEC, FormFactor TRITON, Aehr burn-in) — test-time compression, wafer-measurement-to-packaged-performance correlation models, and independent known-good-die binning/certification for optical engines. First customer profile: a hyperscaler or Broadcom-ecosystem OSAT drowning in the fact that one bad engine among 24+ scraps an expensive CPO assembly.
theses.why_now: Testing is now the loudest bottleneck in CPO mass production (TrendForce): >100s per PIC, no unified standard, manual optical probing, TSMC COUPE ramping 2H 2026. Meta disclosed a 90-million-hour CPO reliability validation — the qualification burden is enormous and hyperscalers will pay to compress it. Keysight paid twice in 12 months (OSG + VPIphotonics) for exactly the link-simulation capability, proving budget exists, but its stack is desktop-era and siloed. Semitronix bought Luceda specifically to fuse design with wafer-test/yield data — validating the loop — yet no independent Western vendor offers it. 2026-2027 first-deployment failure data is about to exist and someone will own it.
theses.market: Wafer-level silicon photonic test systems: ~$670M (2024) → $1.6B (2031, 13.6% CAGR) — but that's hardware; the software/analytics layer on top is greenfield, realistically a 10-20% attach ($100-300M SAM near-term) plus per-wafer-priced test-time-reduction economics that scale with CPO volume (port shipments 50K in 2023 → 4.5M forecast 2027). The digital-twin side sells to perhaps 20 organizations on earth, but at hyperscaler contract sizes ($1-10M/year each). Combined credible ARR path: $20-50M by 2029, with strategic value to Teradyne/Keysight/Advantest far exceeding revenue multiples — Teradyne already bought Quantifi for less capability.
theses.competition: Keysight (VPI Optical Link in ADS — the incumbent link simulator; strong but not cloud-native, not yield-statistical, and conflicted as a test-hardware vendor); Synopsys/Ansys (device-level, weak at system); Teradyne/Quantifi and FormFactor/Advantest/TEL (own the probe hardware and will resist an independent analytics layer — or acquire it); Semitronix/Luceda (the same thesis, but Chinese-owned and thus excluded from US hyperscaler/defense test floors); in-house hyperscaler tools (Meta/Google will build some of this themselves — your counter is cross-vendor breadth).
theses.moat: Data. Correlation models linking wafer-level optical measurements to packaged CPO performance and field reliability only exist if you sit in the flow across multiple foundries/OSATs/customers; each engagement compounds the model. Independence is itself the moat versus Keysight/Teradyne (customers don't want their test-hardware vendor owning their yield data) and versus Semitronix (geopolitics). Standards participation (OIF, OCP, the missing KGD standard) can institutionalize your formats.
theses.capital_intensity: Low-to-moderate. Pure software + physics modeling team (8-15 people); no fab. The catch: credibility requires on-floor deployments, so budget for field application engineers and instrument-adjacent integration work. $5-8M seed to first paid pilot; $25-40M Series A to staff hyperscaler-grade deployments. Fabless in the truest sense.
theses.software_mvp: This week: build an open E-O-E link-budget engine — parameterized models of published CPO components (Broadcom Davisson engine specs, OIF 3.2T module, ELSFP laser specs, ~24.5dBm launch-power budgets, ring modulator thermal sensitivity ~0.072nm/K) with Monte Carlo variation, exposing BER/power/margin via a Python API and web UI. Publish reproductions of public data (NVIDIA's 3.5x power-efficiency claim, Meta's laser-failure statistics) as validation content. That artifact alone opens doors to CPO architecture teams; the test-analytics side follows from the first design partner's wafer data.
risks: Access problem: the data you need lives inside hyperscalers and OSATs who are secretive; without a marquee design partner in year one, the models are toys
Equipment incumbents vertically integrate the analytics layer before you establish it (Teradyne/Quantifi is one product cycle away)
The customer count on the digital-twin side is tiny (~20 buyers); one or two in-house builds at Meta/Google removes a third of the TAM
CPO ramp slips (consensus large-scale deployment is 2028-2030) — you may be 2 years early on the test-volume revenue while burning on hyperscaler sales cycles
Physics-modeling talent for E-O-E co-simulation is scarce and contested by Keysight/Synopsys/NVIDIA

theses.name: Helios Fabric (OCS control plane for the non-Google world)
theses.one_liner: The orchestration and scheduling software that makes reconfigurable optical fabrics actually usable — Google's Apollo topology-engineering stack, productized for everyone buying merchant OCS.
theses.wedge: Software (topology solver, reconfiguration scheduler, ML-job-aware fabric controller, telemetry) that sits between standard cluster schedulers (Kubernetes, Slurm, SLURM-on-cloud, NVIDIA Base Command) and merchant OCS hardware (Lumentum R300, Coherent, Polatis) via the emerging OCP OCS standard. Initial customer: neoclouds and second-tier AI clouds (CoreWeave-class, sovereign AI datacenters) that want Google-style fabric economics — ~108W optical switch vs ~3000W electrical, <3% of system power — but have zero in-house optical networking software capability. Land with a 'fabric efficiency audit' tool; expand to the control plane.
theses.why_now: The hardware is arriving before the software: ~20K OCS units ship in 2026 but Google takes ~18K — the other ~2K are landing at operators with no Apollo equivalent. Lumentum is guiding to ~$100M/quarter OCS revenue by end-2026 and needs its boxes to be deployable; Microsoft already runs OCS in 12 Azure zones (18% rack-power reduction reported); OCP launched OCS standardization with Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA and all major vendors in 2025-26, creating the API surface a third-party control plane can target. SemiAnalysis pegs Apollo's value to Google at >$3B — the software is demonstrably where the value is.
theses.market: Merchant OCS hardware: $0.56B (2026) → ~$2.5B (2029-2032). A control-plane vendor plausibly captures 15-25% of hardware spend as software/subscription (network OS analogy: Arista's EOS economics), so ~$100-500M SAM by 2030 — real but not enormous, and it expands if fast (ns-µs) optical switching for scale-up fabrics materializes (Oriole's PRISM with AMD, 81% core-network power reduction claims), where the same control plane extends to per-collective switching. Honest caveat: Cignal AI explicitly flags OCS-beyond-Google as a possible bubble; this thesis is a call option on a second and third hyperscaler committing.
theses.competition: Google (has the stack, doesn't sell it — but could open-source pieces and kneecap you); the OCS hardware vendors themselves (Lumentum/Coherent/Polatis will ship basic management software; historically optical vendors are bad at cloud-native control planes, but Lumentum has $100M/quarter of motivation); Oriole Networks/iPronics/Salience (funded, but hardware-led — likely partners before competitors); NVIDIA (the existential one: if optical switching enters its reference architectures, its own fabric manager subsumes you); in-house hyperscaler builds (Microsoft already partially built it).
theses.moat: Deployment know-how and integration surface: topology solvers tuned on real traffic traces, qualified interop matrix across OCS vendors and ML schedulers, and OCP-standard leadership. Like all infra control planes, the moat is operational trust accumulated in production — thin at first, thick after ten deployments. Realistically this company wins by becoming the default software partner bundled by Lumentum/Coherent, then is acquired by one of them, Cisco, or Arista.
theses.capital_intensity: Low. Pure software team (6-12) plus a lab with 1-2 OCS units (~$100-300K of hardware — the single meaningful capex item) and GPUs for testbed demos. Seed $4-6M; the constraint is customer access, not capital. Partner with an OCS vendor for lab hardware to cut even that.
theses.software_mvp: This week: a topology-engineering simulator — ingest an AI cluster spec (GPU count, collective patterns, rail-optimized baseline) and traffic traces, solve for OCS-reconfigurable topologies, and output projected job-completion-time and power savings versus static electrical fabrics, calibrated against published Apollo/Azure numbers. This is a pure-Python artifact that doubles as the sales tool: run it on a prospect's cluster telemetry and show them their number. Follow with an OCP-OCS-standard southbound driver stub.
risks: The bubble scenario: no operator besides Google/Microsoft deploys OCS at scale and the merchant market stalls at low hundreds of millions — Cignal AI's warning is explicit
Hardware vendors bundle 'good enough' management software free, compressing you to a services company
NVIDIA reference architectures absorb optical switching and its fabric manager becomes the default control plane
Neocloud customers are cash-constrained and slow to adopt operationally exotic networking
Fast-OCS (the expansion story) is still research-grade; the base business alone may not clear venture scale

theses.name: TrueNorth Photonics (defense PNT silicon photonics, merchant model)
theses.one_liner: Fabless silicon-photonic inertial navigation and timing engines — the second source to Anello and the merchant supplier the FMCW/PNT wave lacks — sold to defense integrators who pay now.
theses.wedge: A navigation-grade silicon-photonic optical gyroscope + IMU module, fabbed on open foundry platforms (Tower PH18/SiN, Ligentec low-loss SiN at <0.5dB/m), sold as a component/module to autonomy primes and integrators (USV/AUV/drone makers like the HavocAI/BlackSea/Vatn cohort Anello already serves, plus European equivalents). Phase two: integrate a chip-scale timing path (PIC comb/narrow-linewidth laser, NIST/Octave lineage) into a combined clock+IMU 'GPS-denied module' — a product no one ships. Deliberately merchant: Anello, Aeva, SiLC, Voyant are all vertically integrated; Tier-1s and primes have no one to design in.
theses.why_now: GPS jamming went from edge case to daily reality (Ukraine, Baltic, Middle East), and defense procurement has caught up: Anello's $20M APFIT production award (Jan 2026) proves DoD is buying photonic gyros in production quantity, not SBIR quantity; its oversubscribed May 2026 round with Lockheed Martin Ventures proves the cap-table appetite. Meanwhile datacom volume has driven SiN/SOI foundry costs down and platforms like Ligentec are automotive-qualified — the cost curve a sensing startup rides for free. Single-vendor risk is already a procurement concern: Anello is effectively alone, and defense buyers structurally demand second sources.
theses.market: Honest sizing: high-performance inertial (FOG/RLG replacement) is ~$1.5-2.5B/year, with the GPS-denied navigation segment growing 15-20% as jamming spreads; chip-scale PNT modules could take $300-600M of it by 2030. This is not a $10B TAM — it is a $50-150M-revenue, high-margin, defensible business with strategic acquirers (Honeywell, Northrop, Collins, Safran, Lockheed) who pay strategic multiples for qualified navigation suppliers. Adjacent expansion (industrial FMCW engines to robotics Tier-1s, timing modules to telecom sync) roughly doubles the SAM.
theses.competition: Anello (the category leader, 5+ years ahead on productization and DoD relationships — you are explicitly the #2); incumbent FOG/RLG vendors (Honeywell, KVH, Exail — better performance today, 10x the size/power/cost, and they are your acquirers more than competitors); MEMS IMU vendors from below (fine for low grade, can't reach navigation grade); Aeva's defense wing and orphaned FMCW assets (Scantinel→MicroVision) on the LiDAR side. The merchant positioning avoids head-on competition with the vertically integrated sensor makers.
theses.moat: Qualification and physics. Navigation-grade optical gyro performance on a foundry SiN process is genuinely hard (loss, drift, bias stability) — a working part is 3-4 years of nonobvious engineering. Defense qualification (MIL-STD, APFIT-style production awards, ITAR-clean US/EU supply via AIM Photonics or European foundries) is a multi-year barrier that also excludes Chinese competition structurally. Design wins in autonomy platforms are sticky for the platform's life.
theses.capital_intensity: Moderate deep-tech, but the capital-efficient kind: fabless on MPW ($30-60K/run on Ligentec/Tower) through prototyping, ~$15-25M to a qualified product, $40-60M cumulative to production scale — Anello's whole history is well under $100M, versus $500M+ for interconnect plays. Government non-dilutive money (SBIR/STTR, APFIT, EDF in Europe) can fund 30-50% of development.
theses.software_mvp: This week: a sensor-fusion and simulation stack ahead of the silicon — an open-architecture GPS-denied navigation engine (factor-graph fusion of IMU/gyro/odometry/vision with jamming-detection), calibrated to published SiPhOG-class error models, sold as software-in-the-loop simulation to autonomy companies evaluating PNT options. It generates revenue and customer intimacy immediately, becomes the firmware of the eventual module, and tells you exactly what gyro spec the market needs before you tape out.
risks: Anello consolidates the category before your part qualifies — being #2 in defense is viable, being #3 is not
Physics risk: foundry SiN waveguide loss and thermal drift may cap you below navigation grade, leaving you in the crowded tactical-grade tier against MEMS
Defense sales cycles: 2-4 years from demo to program of record; bridge financing risk is real
ITAR/export constraints cut you off from commercial scale markets and complicate EU/US dual operations
Incumbent FOG vendors respond with price cuts on legacy product, squeezing the transition window

theses.name: OpenBeam (merchant OCI-MSA optical engine, non-TSMC)
theses.one_liner: The multi-source UCIe-fronted optical engine the hyperscalers just standardized for — built on GlobalFoundries/Tower instead of TSMC, sold to everyone who isn't NVIDIA.
theses.wedge: An OCI-MSA-compliant optical chiplet (UCIe electrical side, parallel CWDM WDM optical side, targeting the standard's path to 3.2Tb/s per link) fabbed on GF Fotonix (monolithic CMOS+photonics, proven with Lightmatter/Ayar) or Tower/OpenLight (integrated lasers), sold to custom-XPU programs — hyperscaler ASIC teams (Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft via Alchip/Broadcom-custom/Marvell-rivals) and AMD-ecosystem players who need optical scale-up but refuse single-vendor lock-in on Ayar Labs or a Marvell subsidiary.
theses.why_now: The OCI MSA (March 2026, founded by AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA, OpenAI) explicitly standardizes a multi-vendor optical scale-up interface — hyperscalers created it precisely because they want second and third sources. Consolidation just deleted the independents: Celestial→Marvell, Nubis→Ciena, DustPhotonics→Credo, Enosemi→AMD. Ayar Labs is the only scaled independent chiplet vendor left, and it just joined NVIDIA's NVLink Fusion orbit — making a neutral alternative more valuable, not less. GF is hungry for anchor photonics customers post-AMF acquisition and will co-invest in enablement.
theses.market: Optical scale-up is the genuinely enormous prize: CPO $8-10B by 2030, with the scale-up tier (GPU-to-GPU/memory) called 'a new market' by LightCounting and validated by Celestial's $3.25B exit and Marvell's claimed ~$10B addressable. A merchant engine vendor winning 2-3 hyperscaler custom-silicon sockets ships millions of chiplets: $500M-1B+ revenue potential by 2030-2032. This is the biggest TAM of any thesis here — and the hardest to reach.
theses.competition: Savage, and mostly better-funded: Ayar Labs ($870M raised, NVIDIA/AMD/Intel all invested, NVLink Fusion member, 5-year head start); Marvell/Celestial (owns the AWS-adjacent custom-XPU channel); Broadcom (will offer OCI engines alongside its custom-ASIC business); Lightmatter (interposer approach, ~$12.5B IPO war chest); Intel's OCI chiplet program; plus TSMC COUPE gravitationally pulling the biggest customers to its ecosystem. You win only on the specific vector of neutrality + non-TSMC supply + OCI-native design — and only if hyperscalers' multi-sourcing rhetoric converts to purchase orders for a startup.
theses.moat: Thin until a design win, then extremely thick: a socket in a hyperscaler XPU program is a 3-5 year committed ramp with co-developed test/packaging flows. Pre-win, the defensible assets are microring/WDM design IP that hits OCI specs on GF's process (nontrivial porting work others haven't done), laser-integration route via OpenLight/Tower that TSMC-ecosystem rivals lack, and the neutrality position itself.
theses.capital_intensity: High — this is honest deep-tech fabless, not lean: $30-50M to a credible sampling chiplet (multiple full mask sets at >$500K each, 4-6 month cycles, packaging/test development, a 40+ person mixed photonics/SerDes team), $150-300M cumulative to production qualification. The Ayar fundraising history ($870M) is the realistic benchmark. Requires a strategic CVC (AMD, a hyperscaler, GF itself) by Series A or don't start.
theses.software_mvp: This week: an OCI-MSA link-compliance and architecture-exploration toolkit — open-source models of the MSA's UCIe+WDM stack, letting XPU architects sweep engine configurations (wavelength counts, launch power vs the ~24.5dBm budget, ring tuning overhead at ~0.12nm/mW) against their bandwidth/pJ-per-bit targets. It builds relationships with the exact 10 architecture teams who will someday buy the chiplet, shapes the spec conversation, and costs nothing but engineering time.
risks: Capital risk dominates: $150M+ before meaningful revenue, in a sector where crossover funding can evaporate with the AI cycle
Hyperscaler multi-sourcing may in practice mean 'Ayar plus Broadcom,' never a startup — the MSA guarantees an interface, not a customer
TSMC COUPE ecosystem lock: if the volume packaging flow standardizes on COUPE, GF-based engines fight uphill on cost/integration
Talent war: microring DWDM + UCIe SerDes engineers are being paid NVIDIA money
Timing: optical scale-up volume is 2028-2030 (Feynman-generation per SemiAnalysis); a 2026 start hits the window only with flawless execution
Acquisition is the likely 'success' outcome, and post-consolidation the buyer list is short (Broadcom won't, Marvell/AMD/Credo already bought)

theses.name: Kelvin Light (athermal high-efficiency multi-wavelength laser source)
theses.one_liner: The bold bet: kill the TEC — an uncooled, high-power, multi-wavelength external laser source that attacks the single largest power and reliability sink in every optical link.
theses.wedge: An ELSFP-form-factor external laser module built around uncooled/athermal multi-wavelength emission (quantum-dot gain, which tolerates 80°C uncooled operation, and/or comb generation) plus zero-static-power wavelength stabilization (photoconductive/PCM-assisted locking instead of brute-force thermoelectric cooling). Target spec: cut ELS wall-plug power 40-60% versus today's DFB+TEC modules at the ~24.5dBm launch powers CPO links require. Sold into the standardized socket the OIF ELSFP and OCI MSA just guaranteed — first customers are CPO switch/system builders (Broadcom ecosystem partners, Celestial/Marvell-class XPU programs) and the hyperscalers who wrote the standards.
theses.why_now: The pain is quantified and public: Meta says ~90% of optical link failures trace to lasers and lasers consume ~60% of link power; lasers+TECs are ~70% of ELS power draw. NVIDIA just paid $4B into Coherent/Lumentum purely for laser supply security — the demand side is desperate. The socket is standardized (ELSFP-02.0, Jan 2025; OCI MSA WDM, Mar 2026), so a component startup doesn't need to win an architecture war. The enabling pieces matured independently: QD-on-Si epi supply chains exist (Quintessent/IQE), Tower/OpenLight offer open-foundry gain integration, comb sources are productizing (Xscape FalconX 8λ), and heaterless ring locking was demonstrated (NewPhotonics). Nobody has assembled 'uncooled + multi-λ + high power + ELSFP' into one module — every light-source startup is attacking a different sub-problem.
theses.market: Lasers/light sources are the largest BOM and power line item in a CPO market going from $46M (2024) to $8-10B (2030), plus the pluggable market (~$26B datacom optics in 2026) where LPO's power story makes efficient lasers equally valuable. If ELS modules are 15-25% of CPO system value, the light-source TAM is $1.5-2.5B by 2030; a startup with a differentiated module taking 10-15% share is a $200-400M revenue business — and the NVIDIA/Coherent/Lumentum dynamic shows laser suppliers now command strategic (not component) valuations.
theses.competition: The most crowded deep-tech lane in the sector, be clear-eyed: Coherent and Lumentum (now NVIDIA-capitalized with purchase commitments — they own today's sockets); the funded startup cohort each holding one piece — Xscape (combs, $81M, Cisco+NVIDIA backing), OpenLight (integrated InP, $84M), Scintil ($58M, NVIDIA), Quintessent (QD, Tower), Aylight (ETH, multiwavelength); Broadcom's internal ELS. Your differentiation must be the system-level power number (module wall-plug efficiency at spec launch power, uncooled), not a device physics claim — if you can't beat Lumentum's next-gen module by >30% in qualified testing, this company shouldn't exist.
theses.moat: Hard-won physics and reliability data: uncooled high-power operation with telecom-grade wavelength stability is a genuine multi-year materials/photonics problem (QD gain dynamics, athermal cavity design, locking electronics), and the resulting qualification corpus (HTOL hours, FIT rates — Intel's 0.09 FIT benchmark is the bar) is the true barrier; hyperscalers qualify lasers over years and don't switch casually. Patents on the athermal stabilization architecture matter here more than in software theses. Post-qualification, laser sockets are among the stickiest in hardware.
theses.capital_intensity: High and unavoidable — this is the deep-tech play: III-V epi runs, hybrid integration development, reliability labs (burn-in racks, HTOL chambers), and 3-4 module generations. ~$15-20M seed/A to a working prototype module (leveraging Tower/OpenLight and IQE-style epi supply rather than owning a fab), $80-150M cumulative through hyperscaler qualification and early production. Comparable trajectory: Xscape at $81M pre-production. Non-negotiable: an NVIDIA/Cisco/hyperscaler strategic in the round, both for validation and for the qualification fast-path.
theses.software_mvp: This week (genuinely useful, not decoration): a laser reliability and link-power modeling platform — physics-based FIT-rate and wavelength-drift models fit to published data (Intel's 45,000-hour HTOL corpus, Meta's failure statistics), plus an ELS power-budget optimizer that shows hyperscalers exactly what an uncooled architecture saves across a 100K-GPU fabric. It sharpens your own spec targets, generates design-partner conversations a year before hardware exists, and its telemetry/health-prediction module becomes the firmware companion product (laser fleet monitoring) once modules ship.
risks: Physics failure mode: uncooled operation may not reach the power+linewidth+stability corner CPO needs; QD output power per wavelength remains the known weakness

Reliability qualification takes 2-3 years of accumulated hours no amount of money compresses — the market may lock in Lumentum/Coherent sockets first, especially with NVIDIA's purchase commitments steering volume
Crowded cap tables: five funded startups plus two NVIDIA-backed incumbents means acquirer supply may exhaust before your exit window
InP/GaAs epi supply chain concentration (China exposure on InP substrates) adds geopolitical input risk
Capital markets risk: this needs $100M+ across a window where photonics funding is hostage to the AI capex cycle; a 2027 AI-spending pause strands the company mid-qualification
Team risk: requires world-class III-V materials + photonics + reliability engineering simultaneously — perhaps 200 people on earth qualify, mostly at Intel/Lumentum/UCSB
